extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate level) intending to get near the boundary of current research in algebraic geometry; not intended for undergraduates or people in other fields
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus and assignment policy for a rigorous, research-oriented graduate course on schemes and foundations of algebraic geometry (Math 216). Covers lecture schedule, problem-set requirements, collaboration policy, and recommended background/readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course scope and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: This course will deal with schemes, and will attempt to be faster and more complete and rigorous than most, but with enough examples and calculations to help develop intuition for the machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are several types of 'introduction to algebraic geometry' and this course focuses on schemes with a rigorous, research-oriented approach; not an examples-only or complex-geometry-only course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience / prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: This course is for mathematicians intending to get near the boundary of current research, in algebraic geometry or a related part of mathematics. It is not intended for undergraduates or people in other fields; for that, people should wait for a later incarnation of Math 216 (which will vary in style over the years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should have sufficient mathematical maturity; if unsure about background, consult recommended references but course isn't designed for casual or cross-field enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: In short, this not a course to take casually. But if you have the interest and time and energy, I will do my best to make this rewarding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should expect a demanding workload and sustained engagement across the quarter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework importance and grading dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike most advanced graduate courses, there will be homework. It is important — this material is very dense, and the only way to understand it is to grapple with it at close range. There will be a problem set most weeks. Your grade will depend on the problem sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem sets are central to learning and to course evaluation; timely completion and quality of problem sets determine grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and attribution policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration is encouraged, but you should give credit for ideas that are not your own. (You will not penalized for that.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with peers is allowed and recommended; explicitly acknowledge contributions from others to avoid academic-misconduct concerns; no penalty for crediting collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat trivial problems / avoid easy exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not do any problems that you already know how to do or that you would find easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students familiar with some material should choose problems that genuinely stretch understanding; this avoids wasting instructor/time and encourages meaningful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative arrangements for experienced students
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have seen some of the material before, and thus don’t have many problems to choose from, please let me know, and we can work out an alternative arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor is open to substituting alternate work or expectations for students with prior exposure to course topics; must be arranged in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-set numeric requirements and due dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem set specifies a number of problems to do (commonly 'Do 10 of the following problems' for many 216A sets; 216B PS1 asks for 'Do 15 of the following problems'; some later sets ask for 'Do 8' or other counts). Each problem set has a stated due date (e.g., Problem set 1 due Friday October 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the per-problem-set instructions: do the required number of problems from the listed items and submit by the listed due date. Counts vary by quarter and by specific problem set; consult each problem-set listing for the exact number and due date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems required to be completed by later deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain problems are labeled 'required to be done by the end of problem set 5' (or other milestone). For example: 'required to be done by the end of problem set 5: 1.3.C, 1.3.G...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some listed problems are mandatory by a specified later problem-set deadline even if not required for the immediate set; track and complete those by the stated milestone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended / particularly recommended / challenge problem labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are sometimes marked as 'particularly recommended', 'strongly recommended', 'challenge problems', or 'required to be done if you haven't seen them before'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these labels to prioritize practice: 'challenge' indicates harder problems for extra credit/skill, 'particularly recommended' highlights especially useful exercises, and conditional requirements indicate prerequisites for those without prior background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection guidance (breadth across sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some problem sets students are instructed to 'Try to do some from each section' or 'Try to do some from each section. (don’t do any you did last week)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting problems, aim for a spread across the covered lecture sections to ensure balanced practice rather than focusing narrowly on one topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and background reading suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended references: Johan de Jong’s stacks project; Hartshorne’s Algebraic Geometry; Mumford’s Red Book of Varieties and Schemes; Qing Liu’s Algebraic Geometry and Algebraic Curves; Gortz and Wedhorn’s Algebraic Geometry I. For commutative algebra: Eisenbud’s Commutative Algebra... or Atiyah and MacDonald. For homological algebra: Weibel’s Introduction to Homological Algebra, Freyd’s Abelian Categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These references are suggested for encyclopedic background, deeper study, or when additional clarity is needed; the notes and stacks project are primary course resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and logistics (time/place, office hours, email list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time and place: Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays 9-10:20 in Hewlett 103 starting Feb. 9. Office hours: Winter quarter Mondays 12:30-2:30, Wednesday 2:30-3:30. 'I have a class email list that I’ll use occasionally... If you are on the list and want to be off it, or vice versa, please let me know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend lectures at stated times/locations; use office hours for help; sign up or opt out of the class email list as desired to receive announcements and corrections.
